item.title: ECB’s Lane says the bar for directional rate guidance is high
item.description:
Comments from the ECB’s Lane on inflation and policy guidance crossed the wires.

  • We put a very high premium on consensus, would be difficult with dots.

  • I would put high bar on directional forward guidance now.

  • Important that ECB has an instrument for multiple equilibriums on bond market.

  • Informative that underlying inflation hasn’t moved yet, it means it’s the usual delayed response.

  • Underlying inflation is a guide to 1-year-ahead inflation.

  • Energy prices already reversing, if that continues you can see headline inflation falling and underlying inflation rising.

  • People should be looking out for whether inflation is coming in stronger or weaker than projections.

Analysis

Lane is keeping his options open on rates. The barometer for traders is how inflation comes in relative to the ECB’s projections, especially if headline and underlying inflation start moving in opposite directions.

Lower energy prices could bring down the headline rate while the earlier shock is still feeding through to underlying inflation. Lane sees underlying inflation as a guide to where inflation could be a year from now. If that measure starts coming in above projections, a softer headline print alone may give the ECB little reason to signal an easier policy path.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stocks mostly higher as hot US CPI sends Treasury yields above 5%
item.description:
As London and European traders head home for the day, the major continental indices are mostly higher, with Spain leading the way. The UK’s FTSE 100 went the other way. In the US, the stronger-than-expected CPI report is still driving the bond and currency markets. The 10-year Treasury yield is back above 5%, the dollar is higher across the board, and an early Nasdaq rebound on Anthropic IPO news has given way to renewed selling.

Spain leads European stocks higher. The FTSE 100 lags.

Spain’s IBEX 35 rose 0.98%, followed by Italy’s FTSE MIB at +0.69%, France’s CAC 40 at +0.55% and Germany’s DAX at +0.31%. The UK’s FTSE 100 fell 0.29%.

European benchmark yields moved higher across the board. France’s 10-year led the move, up 8.5 basis points to 4.806%. Germany rose 7.5 basis points to 3.328%, Spain and Italy each rose 7.4 basis points to 3.896% and 4.380%, respectively, and the UK rose 6.8 basis points to 5.208%.

Hotter US CPI pushes the 10-year back above 5%

October headline CPI rose 0.4% versus 0.3% expected, while core CPI rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected. Headline inflation slowed from September’s 0.6%, but core matched the prior month. On a three-month annualized basis, headline CPI was running at 5.7% and core at 3.7%. The upside surprises gave traders another reason to price in tighter Fed policy after Governor Christopher Waller raised the possibility of a 50-basis-point hike in December.

The US 2-year yield was up 21.4 basis points to 4.761%, the 5-year was up 18.4 basis points to 4.843%, and the 10-year was up 15.5 basis points to 5.017%. The 30-year rose 11.9 basis points to 5.375%. For the rest of the US session, 5% is the barometer for the 10-year. The next thing to watch is whether yields can hold above it.

Waller put 0.3% core CPI in focus before the release

Speaking in London before the CPI report, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he was leaning toward a 25-basis-point hike in December even if inflation cooled in October. If core CPI came in around 0.3% or higher, he said the Fed should consider 50 basis points. His reasoning was that the economy was still growing at a solid pace, the labor market was stable, and inflation was broad enough that moving too slowly could put the Fed’s credibility at risk. Core CPI came in at 0.3%, right around the level he had flagged. That helps explain why the 2-year yield led the move higher, jumping more than 21 basis points to 4.76% by the European close.

Waller also made a point that ties into today’s drop in crude. Oil can fall on hopes for de-escalation in the Middle East, but he said limited refining capacity could keep diesel prices elevated even as crude gets cheaper. For the Fed, the question is how much of those higher energy costs are still feeding through to the prices of other goods and services.

Anthropic gives the Nasdaq a lift, but the gains fade

The Nasdaq indices erased their early losses and briefly moved into positive territory after reports that Anthropic is targeting November 18 to price its IPO and November 19 for its trading debut. Reports indicated that orders already covered the available shares and that roughly 20% of the offering could go to retail investors.

By the European close, the Nasdaq Composite was back down 1.21% and the Nasdaq 100 was down 1.22%. The Dow was down 0.56%, the S&P 500 was down 0.77%, and the Russell 2000 was down 1.18%.

The dollar extends its gains. Gold and silver slide.

EURUSD was down 0.65% at 1.1150 and GBPUSD was down 0.86% at 1.3325. Both pairs moved back below their 200-hour moving averages after CPI. Those averages now give sellers a nearby level to lean against. USDJPY was up 0.56% at 158.79, near its session high of 158.84. AUDUSD was down 1.08% at 0.6851, the largest decline among the major currencies in the snapshot.

Gold was down 2.8% near $4,023 and silver was down 3.9% near $51.32 as yields and the dollar moved higher. Bitcoin was down about 2.6% near $73,020.

Crude oil remains lower, but buyers return from below $84

WTI was down $0.31 at $86.54 after trading as low as $83.88. That puts it $2.66 off the low and within $0.39 of the session high at $86.93. Brent was down $0.64 at $91.93 after dipping to $89.16.

On the Middle East front, President Trump played down the prospect of renewed major strikes against Iran after meeting with Qatar’s prime minister on Monday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reinforced that message on Tuesday, saying the administration saw less need for major combat operations while sanctions and the naval blockade remained in place. Iran’s top security official said no negotiations with Washington were underway, and the Strait of Hormuz remained a sticking point. The softer US tone helped take some of the supply risk premium out of crude early, but both benchmarks had recovered much of their losses by the European close.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran's Rezaei: No negotiations currently taking place between Tehran and Washington
item.description:
The comments today from Rubio and Rezaei don't sound like there is any possibility of a deal. So it looks like it's back to some kind of war of economic attrition, with the US attempting to blockade Iran while Iran tries to drive the price of oil higher with the help of Houthis in Yemen.

How that goes depends on how effective you think Iran will be in disrupting shipping in Hormuz. Today, France's Macron was out with talk about improving insurance rates in Hormuz. It's also not clear how much oil is getting out of the gulf via alternative routes, not to mention oil products and other commodities.

At the same time, I'm not sure how much weight you can put on public comments from Rezaei, Rubio or anyone involved.

From Rezaei:

  • Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until US meet's Iran's seven conditions
  • All US claims regarding continuation of negotiations with Iran are pure lies and fabrications
  • We asked the US to provide a clear response to our proposals
  • US hasn't provided a clear response yet but they might provide such a response in the future

What makes me most skeptical about his credibility are his denial of negotiations. There have been so many reports of planes flying between Iran and elsewhere, that's a laughable line.

WTI is down 22-cents to $86.70 but the momentum in talks is clearly lost and I see clear upside risks from here.

Rezaei is the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin tests its 200 day moving average after hotter US CPI data
item.description:
Hotter CPI gives Bitcoin sellers another push

Bitcoin was trading near $74,300 ahead of the US CPI release and fell to around $73,500 in the minutes that followed. That put it down about 2% from Monday’s close in early US trading.

Headline CPI rose 0.4% versus 0.3% expected, while core CPI rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected. The market was already pricing in a 25-basis-point hike in December, and the stronger numbers brought a 50-basis-point move more into play. The US 2-year yield rose about 19 basis points to 4.74%, the 10-year yield climbed 13 basis points to 4.991%, and the dollar moved higher. That combination added to the pressure on Bitcoin.

ETF outflows had already put Bitcoin on the defensive

US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $201 million in net outflows on Monday, the third straight session of withdrawals. Sellers already had the upper hand heading into the CPI release.

The 200-day moving average is the barometer

Recall that Bitcoin came within a few hundred dollars of its 200-day moving average on both Sunday and Monday. The price bounced on Monday, but that rally had a limit. It stalled near $75,480, inside the swing area between $74,925 and $76,052.

Today’s rotation lower has taken Bitcoin above and below its 200-day moving average at $73,134. The price reached a low of $72,787 and is trading at $73,092 at the time of writing, just below the moving average.

If buyers can get and stay back above $73,134, they would take some of the immediate pressure off. From there, the next upside target is $74,925, the lower end of the swing area where Monday’s rally stalled.

What would give sellers more control?

The next downside target is $72,554, the 50% midpoint of the rally from the early July low to the September high. If sellers can keep the price below the 200-day moving average and get and stay below that midpoint, they would have more control.

Below the midpoint, there is little obvious support before the 61.8% retracement at $69,057.

In the video above, I walk through the technicals driving Bitcoin and outline the levels buyers and sellers are watching next.

Trading education. Watch what happens after the break

When the price keeps crossing a moving average, the next retest can tell you which side is gaining control. If a bounce stalls below $73,134, sellers have a nearby level to lean against while they look for a test of $72,554. If buyers reclaim the moving average and hold it on a pullback, the move below it starts to look like a failed break. Either way, the retest gives traders a clear level for defining risk.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Logan: It's clear that Fed needs at least two more quarter-point rate hikes
item.description:
Logan is a hawk and has dissented in favor of hikes so her comments might not be as hawkish as feared after what we heard today from Waller:

  • Excess inflation is unacceptable
  • Clear that Fed needs at least two more quarter-percentage-point rate increases
  • Says it may be possible to raise interest rates more rapidly this winter than US central bank has moved so far
  • Important to ‘promptly’ achieve balance in outlook, risks for inflation and employment
  • Adjusting policy gradually can reduce risk that economic activity deteriorates more sharply than necessary
  • After two more rate hikes, it would make sense to pause and assess what further action may be appropriate
  • Higher bond-market rates signal monetary policy has work to do, not an independent tailwind for activity
  • Fed policy rate is at least 50 basis points below a modestly restrictive level
  • Accommodative policy is adding to inflationary pressures; real Fed funds rate is 78 basis points, data suggest
  • Wartime energy disruptions not the only source of price pressures
  • Concerned that higher-than-expected consumer price index means personal consumption expenditures inflation could rise
  • Inflation is trending meaningfully higher than 2% goal
  • Labor market is balanced and even tightening a bit
  • Economic growth is strong, consumer spending solid, business spending robust
  • Price pressures also broader than tariffs, and broad trend is likely to persist

The whole market is repricing Fed action today, basically adding another hike to the next 12 months picture in light of comments from Waller and the CPI data. You can see that in two-year yields as well, which are up 20 basis points on the day to 4.75%. There is this growing chorus that the current Fed funds rate of 3.75-4.00% isn't holding back the economy, in part due to intense AI capex. The thing is, by the time the Feds rate peaks (priced for H2 2027, the AI capex could be starting to dry up.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US 2-year yields surge as the market realizes the US has an inflation problem
item.description:
The bond market is kicking and screaming again.

US 2-year yields are up 19 basis points to 4.73% as the market digests a hut CPI report and comments from Chris Waller. The Fed Governor said that a 50 basis points hike was on the table for December if core CPI ran at +0.3% or higher. Well it was at 0.3% and if not for a 1.2% drop in monthly used auto prices, then it would have been +0.4%. Waller also highlighted the widening breadth of price increases and that was evident in the report.

This month, the market had grown less worried about inflation because oil prices have fallen but the Fed thinking is that inflationary expectations are starting to get built into 2027 price setting. That's something I highlighted in late October, as Whirlpool said it would hike price 7% starting December 3.

The Fed was wrong when it said that tariff effects would move through the economy quickly and now we're seeing that. Companies like Whirlpool saw margins collapse and tried to avoid price hikes. Consumers had also benchmarked on lower prices and some income segments are certainly struggling but eventually vendors realize they have to hike prices as the costs of things like steel and other inputs move through the supply chain.

I think the Fed is getting that rude awakening right now. Oil prices have obviously come down but product cracks are stiill absurdly wide so that limits the downside for now. I can't see that materially improving unless we get peace in the Middle East and Ukraine. There have been some positive steps recently but there's no sign a concluded deal on either front is imminent, so I'd argue that risks are towards sentiment worsening.

Here is what Marco Rubio, the US Secretary of State, said today:

At the moment, the talks have not been particularly productive because the Iranian demands are simply unacceptable, and in some cases they are outrageous, ridiculous, and detached from reality... We're not going to pay. Iran, you know, is demanding reparations. They should be the ones paying reparations because they're the ones that have, you know, destabilized the region for long periods of time. They're demanding pallets of cash, which the president made clear is not going to happen. If they want a nuclear energy program, they should have one, like many other countries around the world have. So there's things they can do, but just right now they just don't seem, you know, at that point. Now I think they want a deal. There's no doubt they'd like a deal too, but they're just not ready to make one apparently. But we're open to a little bit changes. But I don't think status quo is the right way to phrase this. Status quo means that things are going to stay static. They're not. They're going to continue to grow. What I'm saying to you is that the economic campaign is so devastating that right now there really is no need for major combat operations. The president has basically said that over the last few days, and that's what I told our European allies today.

That doesn't sound great.

So as the election dust settles, it's starting to look like nothing will change and that's problematic and inflationary. I would also argue that at some point you will have to price in a Democratic sweep in 2028 and all the fiscal largess that will come with it, if Republicans don't force some kind of strategy change on Iran or tariffs.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stocks slide, yields jump, USD higher after hotter-than-expected October CPI

October details compared with September, seasonally adjusted

  • Energy +0.7% vs +5.2%. Gasoline rose 1.0% after September’s 9.1% jump, but electricity accelerated to +0.9% from +0.2%.

Headline inflation slowed as the rise in gasoline prices moderated, but core CPI rose 0.3% for a third straight month. Quick analysis

A move back above the respective averages would weaken the bearish bias and put the breaks at risk of failing.

What this report measures

The Consumer Price Index tracks what households pay for goods and services. Core CPI excludes food and energy. The three-month annualized rate shows how much prices would rise over a year if the latest three-month pace continued and given Wallers comments, can bring in a 50 bp hike in December.  One could argue that the Fed absent the election, should have hiked in October but held off for political reasons. Nevertheless, the 12% number for 50 bps is still low.

item.title: US October core CPI +0.3% vs +0.2% expected
item.description:
• Prior core m/m was +0.3%
  • Core unrounded +0.297%
  • Core CPI y/y not published vs +2.6% prior
  • Core unrounded y/y not published vs +2.564% prior
  • Headline CPI m/m +0.4% vs +0.3% expected (prior +0.6%)
  • Headline CPI y/y not published vs 3.7% prior
  • Unrounded not published vs +3.738% prior
  • Core goods +0.2% vs +0.3% m/m prior
  • Real weekly earnings 0.0% vs -0.5% prior (revised to -0.4%)
  • Supercore m/m roughly +0.4%, with just over half driven by services less energy services

Key sub-components:

  • Owners’ equivalent rent: +0.3% vs +0.3% prior
  • Rent of primary residence: +0.2% vs +0.2% prior
  • Motor vehicle insurance: +0.7% vs +0.1% prior
  • Airfares: +0.4% vs +1.2% prior
  • Used cars: -1.2% vs +0.7% prior
  • Apparel: +0.1% vs +0.3% prior
  • Medical care: +0.3% vs +0.1% prior
  • Lodging away from home: +0.6% vs +2.0% prior
  • Energy m/m: +0.7% vs +5.2% prior
  • Gasoline m/m: +1.0% vs +9.1% prior
  • Food m/m: +0.5% vs 0.0% prior
  • New vehicles: +0.2% vs +0.2% prior

Note that the BLS did not collect survey data for October 2025 because of a lapse in appropriations during the government shutdown. That also makes many of the numbers impossible to calculate.

Summing the BLS contribution table (food 0.064, energy 0.053, core 0.234) gives about +0.35% unrounded, which makes the headline number a tad better than it looks.

Following Waller's hawkish comments, the market is fully priced for a December hike and is pricing in 60 bps of hiking in the year ahead. USD/JPY was trading at 158.19 ahead of the data and 158.44 afterawrds. S&P 500 futures were flat but down 0.7% afterwards. US 2-year yields were up 9 bps ahead of the data and +13 bps afterwards.

Waller said a half-point hike might be needed in December if core CPI comes in "around 0.3% or higher". That raised the stakes on today's report. He also said, he would support quarter-point rate hike in December even if October CPI improves versus September. Notably, he said he was particularly concerned about the breadth of price increases.

Looking through the data, the breadth shows up in supercore at +0.4%. Used cars and communications were “among the small number of major indexes that decreased," the BLS wrote. Core goods ex-used cars rose 0.4% and core ex-shelter and used cars rose 0.4%, both the largest since January. Used car prices fell 1.2% m/m in October and without that, this report would have been ugly at +0.4% in all the key metrics instead of +0.3%.

Furnishings and supplies rose 0.7%, the largest since June 2025. Furniture was +1.2%, appliances +1.3%, tools and hardware +1.4%, and housekeeping supplies +0.9% (largest since January 2023). Transportation services were up 0.8%, the largest since January. Insurance was +0.7%, maintenance and repair +0.6%, and public transportation +2.0%.

For background, the Consumer Price Index from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics is the most market-moving inflation report in the world. It’s released monthly at 8:30 am ET, usually in the second week of the following month, and measures changes in the prices urban consumers pay for a basket of goods and services, including food, energy, shelter, vehicles, apparel, medical care, transportation and recreation.

Unlike Canada, where the focus is the unadjusted annual rate, US markets zero in on the seasonally adjusted monthly change, particularly in core CPI, which excludes food and energy. Traders often calculate the unrounded figures from the index levels, because the difference between a 0.24% and a 0.26% monthly gain can decide whether the print rounds up or down and how markets react.

Shelter is the largest component, at roughly a third of the overall index. It’s dominated by owners’ equivalent rent, an estimate of what homeowners would pay to rent their own homes, along with rent of primary residence. Because shelter is measured through leases that turn over slowly, it lags market rents by many months.

Markets also watch supercore inflation, core services excluding housing, which is seen as the best gauge of wage-driven price pressures. Volatile categories such as airfares, used cars, motor vehicle insurance and lodging away from home frequently drive surprises.

The Federal Reserve targets 2% inflation on the PCE price index rather than CPI, but CPI comes first and several components feed directly into PCE. Combined with PPI, it lets economists estimate core PCE before it’s released. A surprise in core CPI can move Treasury yields, the US dollar and equities sharply and shift rate expectations ahead of the next FOMC meeting.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

What has been reported

As reported by the New York Times on 29th October, US authorities suspect a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company, of working for China’s Ministry of State Security, and Huang may have been the target of a Chinese espionage effort. According to the Times, Megaspeed bought about $4.8 billion of NVIDIA hardware over two years. According to CBS News, NVIDIA’s board announced on Sunday 8th November that a committee of independent directors, working with outside counsel, will investigate, and Huang has said he will cooperate fully.

The investigation is ongoing and no findings have been published. China has rejected them as groundless, according to CBS News, and NVIDIA’s board has said it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. Huang remains chief executive. The board has said it has confidence in him.

Shareholders filed a proposed class action on Monday 9th November, according to Reuters. The complaint, filed in federal court in San Jose, California, according to The Week, alleges that NVIDIA and Huang failed to disclose his reported ties to the former Megaspeed executive. These are allegations that have not been tested in court. President Donald Trump has said the FBI is looking into the matter, according to Reuters. No FBI statement has been reported.

Why it matters for the shares

The risk investors are weighing is less NVIDIA's revenue than governance and policy. item.title: Chart of the day: Nasdaq comeback looks to have the breadth but does it have the staying power?
item.description:
The dip buyers are back in town and seeing how yesterday played out, they've apparently decided that last week's tech selloff was a rather generous early Christmas sale. The Nasdaq closed up by 2.7% to start the new week, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) surged by nearly 6.9%. That's quite the comeback after a rather brutal showing by tech stocks in the week before.

But before we get too carried away with the latest rebound, it is worth asking whether this is the start of another meaningful rally or just the market picking itself up after falling flat on its face? The chart below offers some perspective.

Despite Monday's impressive recovery, the Nasdaq is still slightly below where it finished October trading. Meanwhile, semiconductor stocks remain roughly 6% below their levels at the end of last month - having suffered a rather punishing 12% decline just last week.

Overall, what we're seeing is not all too surprising. After all, the sharper the fall, the more spectacular the rebound can look.

That being said, there is at least something encouraging beneath the surface.

AMD surged higher by 13.3% and Broadcom climbed by 8.8% in trading yesterday, while 29 out of 30 semiconductor index constituents finished higher.

The lone exception? Well, taht was Nvidia. The poster boy of the AI trade fell by over 4% yesterday but that was largely tied to the controversy surrounding CEO Jensen Huang rather than a straightforward reflection of broader AI demand.

As such, I'm not going to lump Nvidia's decline together with the wider semiconductor story. If anything, the sector's ability to rally strongly despite weakness in its biggest name is an encouraging sign that buying interest extends beyond just one company.

So, what's the catch here?

Strong breadth tells us that buyers are returning to the market. However, it doesn't necessarily tell us that they'll be sticking around.

For the Nasdaq, it will be important to watch to see if dip buyers can hold above the 200-day moving average after reclaiming the key technical level yesterday. For semiconductor stocks, the challenge is arguably even greater. The SOX remains below its own 200-day moving average and so that leaves plenty of ground to make up despite Monday's surge.

If both can start overcoming these technical hurdles while broader market participation holds up, then we might have a stronger case that this recovery has legs beyond Monday's bargain hunting.

The US CPI report today provides the next meaningful test, particularly if hotter inflation reinforces expectations of a December Fed rate hike. And Fed governor Waller has just raised the stakes after suggesting that a core monthly inflation reading of 0.3% or higher could warrant considering a larger 50 bps rate hike in December.

For now, the comeback looks convincing enough for one day. However, getting buyers back through the door is arguably the easy part. Keeping them around though? That's where the real test begins.

item.title: Stock earnings pick of the week: Can Applied Materials spot cracks in the AI spending boom?
item.description:
Spend, spend, spend. That's been the name of the game in the AI boom over the past two years. But really, just how much longer can the industry keep throwing money at bigger and better chips before someone starts asking whether the returns are worth it? Well, Applied Materials might give us a few clues this week.

The semiconductor equipment giant reports earnings on Thursday this week. And just like the rest of the other tech earnings these days, I would be less interested in whether it can beat Wall Street's estimates. Instead, I'd focus much more on what the company has to say about the next round of spending.

I mean you would think that if the AI investment frenzy is beginning to lose steam, then the companies supplying the tools to build those chips might be among the first to notice.

Everyone loves a gold rush, especially the folks selling the shovels. And in the AI boom, Applied Materials is very much in the business of selling those shovels.

Wall Street is expecting revenue of $10.30 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $4.06, compared with $6.80 billion and $2.17 respectively a year ago. That's quite a big leap and one that speaks to the relentless spending on advanced chips and manufacturing capacity.

For some context, Applied Materials delivered record revenue of $9.12 billion in the previous quarter with non-GAAP earnings per share of $3.50. At the time, the management laid out an ambitious longer-term outlook, expecting wafer fabrication equipment spending to grow faster through 2030 than over the past decade. However, we have seen how things can quickly change in the past quarter with other big tech firms. So, this is where things might get a little tricky.

The bottom line now is that strong AI demand doesn't automatically guarantee that the current pace of capital expenditure is sustainable.

Chipmakers are pouring money into manufacturing, high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging. And Applied Materials sits right in the middle of that spending cycle, supplying the equipment needed to make these growingly more complex chips.

As such, I'll be watching whether the management continues to see accelerating demand from leading-edge foundry and DRAM customers. Besides that, any indication that orders or capacity expansion plans are being pushed further into 2027 will also be a key signal to watch this week.

But perhaps most importantly is the question of will customers keep spending at this pace if the returns on AI infrastructure investment take longer to materialise?

A more confident outlook could lend support to semiconductor equipment names and the wider AI trade in broader markets. However, any suggestion of slowing investment commitments could revive concerns over how much optimism is already priced into tech stocks.

As has been the case in the past month, markets have come to terms that the AI boom has already delivered plenty of impressive numbers. What they need now is more concrete evidence that the spending can keep going without eventually running ahead of the returns.

And that's the same narrative in play when looking at Applied Materials' earnings this week.

item.title: Fed's Waller says a half-point rate hike in December may be needed if Core CPI comes in hot
item.description:
• Half-point Fed rate hike may be needed in December, if October Core CPI inflation comes in around 0.3% or higher
  • Would support quarter-point rate hike in December even if October CPI improves vs September
  • US inflation is too high, September's inflation data was bad
  • Was willing to wait on policy tightening in October; what matters is that promised hikes are delivered in a reasonable period of time
  • Particularly concerned about the breadth of price increases
  • Suspect GDP growth is backing off in current quarter, but output will continue to grow at solid pace
  • Fed staff analyses suggest more producer price increases ahead, and potential for energy price shock to be more persistent
  • Labor market solid, supply and demand roughly in balance, employment close to Fed's goal
  • Unclear if labour market is as healthy as the unemployment rate suggests; dynamism and productivity growth questions need more research

These are very hawkish remarks from Fed's governor Waller as he's suggesting that a rate hike in December would be warranted regardless of today's inflation data. The only thing that the data would change for him is the magnitude of the increase as a Core CPI M/M at 0.3% or higher would lead him to vote for a larger 0.5% hike. 

Waller stressed that US inflation remains too high and described September's inflation report as disappointing. He had been willing to wait on further policy tightening at the October meeting, but emphasised that what matters now is delivering the promised rate hikes within a reasonable period of time. He also highlighted concerns about the breadth of price increases, suggesting that inflationary pressures remain more widespread than he would like.

He acknowledged that GDP growth may be slowing in the current quarter, although he still expects output to expand at a solid pace. He noted that Fed staff analyses point to further producer price increases ahead and warned that the energy price shock could prove more persistent than initially expected.

Regarding the labour market, Waller described conditions as broadly solid, with supply and demand roughly in balance and employment close to Fed's objectives. However, he cautioned that the unemployment rate alone may not fully capture the health of the labour market, pointing to questions surrounding labour market dynamism and productivity growth that require further analysis.

Keep in mind that Waller is a very influential governor and has been a leading indicator for Fed's policy since 2021. He's been willing to give disinflation a chance back in September but has now drastically changed his mind. The probabilities for a December hike jumped to 99% following Waller's comments (the 1% is for a 0.5% hike).

It's a sea of green for European equities with gains of over 1% across most major indices. Lower oil prices are offering some welcome relief to the inflation outlook, particularly for Europe given its exposure to imported energy costs. So, that is giving investors a reason to reassess the economic damage from the recent energy shock over the past few months.

That being said, I'd be careful about getting too carried away with the optimism. Falling oil prices may be taking some pressure off the inflation outlook but that doesn't necessarily mean the broader problem is going away just yet.

And with the US CPI report coming up later today, we could get yet another reminder of just how much work central banks might still have ahead of them.

Headline inflation is expected to slow to 0.3% m/m in October, down from 0.6% in September. Meanwhile, core inflation is estimated to ease to 0.2% m/m - down from 0.3% previously. Markets are still pricing roughly an 84% probability of another Fed rate hike in December, so that leaves little room for an upside inflation surprise.

For European equities, I would argue that the bigger risk isn't necessarily the inflation numbers themselves. It is more about how US Treasury yields react afterwards. A hotter report could send yields higher, revive concerns over tighter financial conditions and take some shine off the rally in equities. On the flip side, softer inflation alongside falling oil prices could give buyers another reason to extend the recovery.

For now though, dip buyers are still holding the upper hand. But with the US CPI report still to come, there is every reason for markets to heed some caution.

item.title: Macro pulse: Wall Street's relief rally is looking good but what happens next?
item.description:
Wall Street is certainly enjoying itself again to start the new week. The S&P 500 surged by 2.3% yesterday, its best performance since April, as falling oil prices and hopes of a de-escalation in the US-Iran war gave investors a reason to pile back into stocks.

Fair enough. Cheaper oil prices help to take some pressure off inflation, which then eases the squeeze on corporate costs and household spending. So, that's good news for stocks especially after the brutal selloff last week.

But now, what happens when all that optimism is starting to get priced into markets? Let's think about if for a second. A potential end to the Middle East conflict removes one major source of uncertainty for equities. However, it doesn't necessarily give stocks a fresh catalyst to keep pushing higher endlessly.

As such, I would argue that there are three things worth watching to judge whether this latest rebound has any staying power.

The first one is that Treasury yields need to also play along.

10-year Treasury yields are hovering just below 4.90% and that's hardly an invitation for investors to throw caution to the wind. If oil prices keep falling but bond yields remain elevated, any real benefit to equity valuations could prove to be limited once the dust settles.

Adding to that, Washington's fiscal outlook isn't helping either. Persistent deficits and heavy borrowing requirements could continue to underping long-term yields especially, even as geopolitical risks fade.

Besides that, cheaper oil alone isn't going to change the Fed's thinking overnight. Markets are still pricing in roughly an 84% chance of a December rate hike, so there are still some hawkish undertones for traders to manage. The first test of which will come later today from the US CPI report.

The second thing is to see whether the equities rally can broaden beyond the usual suspects.

The rebound yesterday was definitely encouraging, with all 11 sectors of the finishing higher and the Russell 2000 gaining by 3.1%. The question now though is can that very momentum continue?

If small caps, industrials and consumer discretionary stocks keep participating, that would suggest investors are buying into a healthier economic outlook rather than simply chasing another technology rebound. As for a rally that is carried by fewer and fewer stocks? Well, that's a completely different story.

And lastly, earnings also need to pull their weight and justify the enthusiasm.

Now, the AI spending debate hasn't disappeared just because oil prices are falling. Investors still need a lot of convincing that the enormous capex commitments will eventually translate into sustainable profit growth. But if valuations keep rising faster than earnings expectations, we're only likely to see the market turn to become more vulnerable to another disappointment.

So, that is the broader picture that I'll be watching next even as geopolitical tensions start to ease from hereon.

A genuine de-escalation in the US-Iran war could certainly lay the groundwork for a sustained recovery. However, I'd also want to see falling bond yields, broader equity participation and stronger earnings expectations to reinforce that optimism.

Otherwise, we could end up with a case of market players already buying into the good news but haven't quite figured out what comes next. And that's when the easy part of the rally comes to an end.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Learn technical analysis without being a professor: This repeating pattern is super simple and super effective
item.description:
Gold futures: A breakout, a retest, and another move higher

You don't need to be a professor to learn technical analysis. This simple pattern on gold's 4-hour chart offers a valuable lesson about identifying the stronger side of the market, even if you use a completely different trading strategy.

My 4-hour gold chart from today, November 10, is super simple. No indicators, zero noise. And I can tell you that once you practice recognizing these patterns, they can become an extremely useful part of your trading analysis.

But let's clarify something first.

"Effective" does NOT mean you will always profit.

Patterns matter because they give you guidance about which side of the market is currently stronger. That can help you develop an edge, although no particular win rate is guaranteed. Experience, confirmation, execution and risk management all matter.

It also doesn't mean prices cannot change direction later, that other patterns don't matter, or that something unexpected won't happen five minutes from now and change the market entirely.

With that in mind, let's look at gold.

Gold's 4-hour chart: Three simple observations

Gold futures had been moving lower inside a channel, between two downward-sloping lines.

Some traders would look at this as a potential bullish continuation pattern, similar to a bull flag.

Now look at the three numbered points on the chart.

Point 1: The breakout

Gold moved above the upper line of the descending channel.

This is called a breakout.

It's the first indication that buyers may be becoming stronger and that the downward structure could be ending.

But a breakout doesn't automatically mean prices will continue rising. Sometimes they fail, and prices return inside the original channel.

That's why the next observation is important.

Point 2: The retest

After the breakout, gold moved lower and returned to the channel line it had previously crossed.

This is called a retest, and it happens quite often in financial markets.

The idea is simple. An area that previously acted as resistance, making it difficult for prices to move higher, may later become support, where buyers are willing to step in.

In this case, gold returned to the breakout area around $4,050-$4,070 and then moved higher again.

That's another positive sign for the bulls.

Point 3: The move higher continues

After the retest, gold started moving higher again.

At the time of the chart, gold futures were trading near $4,130.

The next area I'm watching is around $4,150-$4,160.

If gold breaks above this area and can hold there, that would provide further evidence that buyers remain in control.

On the other hand, a move back inside the old descending channel would weaken the bullish interpretation.

So, for now, the bulls appear stronger than the bears on this timeframe. That doesn't mean I know what gold will do next. It means the available price structure favors one side over the other.

A different way to look at bull flags and bear flags

Traditionally, technical analysts identify a bull flag as a strong upward move (the pole), followed by downward-sloping consolidation and a potential breakout higher. A classic bear flag is the opposite.

But many years ago, I learned an interesting approach from a market expert who already had 15 years of experience.

Look at almost every ascending channel as a potential bear flag, and almost every descending channel as a potential bull flag.

That's something I still do today.

The keyword is potential.

A descending channel becomes more interesting to bulls when price breaks above it. An ascending channel becomes more interesting to bears when price breaks below it.

But here's where it gets particularly interesting.

If an ascending channel breaks upwards instead, that's an especially bullish development. And if a descending channel breaks downwards, that's an especially bearish development.

Why? Because instead of reversing the previous direction of the channel, price demonstrates enough strength or weakness to break out in that same direction.

These aren't necessarily textbook flags, and a breakout alone doesn't guarantee a sustained move. But observing whether price breaks out, fails, or successfully retests a channel can provide extremely useful information.

Why learn these patterns if you already have a trading strategy?

You don't have to trade bull flags or draw trendlines as part of your own strategy.

Maybe you prefer moving averages, VWAP, Fibonacci levels, order flow or something completely different.

That's fine.

But recognizing common price patterns gives you another perspective on what the market is doing.

For example, suppose your trading strategy gives you a signal to buy.

If the larger chart also shows a successful bullish breakout, a retest and a continuation higher, you have additional evidence supporting that direction.

Now imagine the opposite.

Your strategy tells you to sell, but the larger chart shows buyers repeatedly defending support and pushing prices higher.

Wouldn't that be useful information to consider before entering a short position?

It doesn't necessarily mean your strategy is wrong. It means you have another piece of evidence to evaluate.

And that's the main lesson I want to share.

You don't need to change your trading strategy to benefit from understanding other methods.

Learn to recognize patterns. Watch what happens when they break out, when they fail and when prices return to test important areas.

Over time, this can help you better understand which side of the market has the advantage, identify potential opportunities and recognize when the evidence is changing.

For gold right now, the 4-hour chart tells a fairly simple story: breakout, retest, continuation. Buyers have shown greater strength.

Could that change? Absolutely.

But until the price action tells us otherwise, there's no reason to ignore what the chart is showing us.

Patterns matter. And sometimes, keeping things simple is the best place to start.

--------------------------------

According to the latest technical breakdown at investingLive.com, gold's 4-hour chart continues to flash a simple yet highly effective repeating pattern that active traders should be watching closely.

The current structure clearly shows that bulls have the upper hand over bears, keeping gold's price action skewed to the upside amid a favorable macro backdrop.

While market conditions can always shift, betting against this momentum right now is a losing proposition, as pattern recognition remains critical.

This bullish resilience is especially notable given the broader headwinds across the commodities space, standing firm even as major institutions revise their broader outlook, such as the recent update where Goldman Sachs cut its 2026 and 2027 gold targets due to a hawkish Fed.
